cards.front: What do the acronyms LIFO and FIFO stand for?
cards.back: Last In First Out (stack) and First In First Out (queue)
cards.extra: A stack pops the youngest element it received; a queue polls the oldest. Both are built on the same three operations: add, remove, peek.
cards.example:
java.util.Deque stack = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();   // LIFO: Last In First Out
java.util.Queue queue = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();   // FIFO: First In First Out
stack.push("a"); stack.push("b"); queue.add("a"); queue.add("b");
System.out.println(stack.pop() + " " + queue.remove());   // b then a

cards.front: Which element does Deque.pop() remove, and which one does Deque.poll() remove?
cards.back: pop() removes the head, poll() also removes the head
cards.extra: They differ only in the empty case: pop() throws NoSuchElementException, poll() returns null. Stack behaviour built on a deque uses push/pop, which act on the same end.
cards.example:
java.util.Deque d = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();
d.addLast("head"); d.addLast("tail");
System.out.println(d.pop());   // head: pop removes the head
System.out.println(d.poll());  // tail, now the head: poll removes the head too

cards.front: In the Queue interface, which method throws and which returns a special value for a failed add?
cards.back: add() throws IllegalStateException; offer() returns false
cards.extra: Same pairing everywhere in Queue: throwing variant on add/poll/peek is add/remove/element, value-returning variant is offer/poll/peek.
cards.example:
java.util.Queue q = new java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1);
q.add("one");
System.out.println(q.offer("two"));   // false: special value for failed add
try { q.add("two"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("add throws"); }

cards.front: In the Queue interface, which method throws and which returns a special value when the queue is empty?
cards.back: remove() and element() throw NoSuchElementException; poll() and peek() return null
cards.extra: So the optionals come in pairs: remove/poll both take an element, element/peek both look at one. Only the failure behaviour differs.
cards.example:
java.util.Queue q = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();
try { q.remove(); } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException e) { System.out.println("remove throws"); }
try { q.element(); } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException e) { System.out.println("element throws"); }
System.out.println(q.poll() + " " + q.peek());   // null null: special values

cards.front: What does Deque add to Queue?
cards.back: Operations on both ends (head and tail), so one type models a queue and a stack
cards.extra: Deque stands for double ended queue. The Queue method names are kept, and a new suffix convention (First/Last) duplicates them for each end.
cards.example:
java.util.Deque both = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();
both.addLast("q1"); both.addLast("q2"); System.out.println(both.pollFirst());   // queue: FIFO, tail ops
both.addFirst("s1"); both.addFirst("s2"); System.out.println(both.pollFirst());   // stack: LIFO, head ops
System.out.println(both);   // one type, operations on both ends

cards.front: Map a FIFO push onto the Deque suffix convention: which method throws and which returns a value?
cards.back: addLast() throws IllegalStateException; offerLast() returns false
cards.extra: Deque mirrors Queue exactly: add/offer become addLast/offerLast, remove/poll become removeFirst/pollFirst, element/peek become getFirst/peekFirst.
cards.example:
java.util.Deque d = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>(1);
d.addLast("one");
System.out.println(d.offerLast("two"));   // false: special value for failed FIFO push
try { d.addLast("two"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("addLast throws"); }

cards.front: Which two methods give LIFO push behaviour on a Deque?
cards.back: addFirst() (throws) and offerFirst() (returns false)
cards.extra: Pushing at the head means the youngest element is also the first one, which is what makes pop() and poll() on the head a stack pop.
cards.example:
java.util.Deque d = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>(1);
d.addFirst("one");
System.out.println(d.offerFirst("two"));   // false: special value for failed LIFO push
try { d.addFirst("two"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("addFirst throws"); }

cards.front: Which Deque method names replace Queue.element() and Queue.peek()?
cards.back: getFirst() and peekFirst()
cards.extra: The one naming exception in the convention: the peek family became getFirst/getLast, not element. getFirst throws on an empty deque, peekFirst returns null.
cards.example:
java.util.Deque d = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();
d.add("h"); System.out.println(d.getFirst() + " " + d.peekFirst());   // both look at the head
d.clear(); System.out.println(d.peekFirst());   // null on empty
try { d.getFirst(); } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException e) { System.out.println("getFirst throws"); }

cards.front: Name the three non-concurrent implementations of Queue/Deque in the Collections Framework.
cards.back: ArrayDeque, LinkedList (both interfaces), and PriorityQueue (Queue only)
cards.extra: ArrayDeque is array-backed and grows on demand; LinkedList is node-backed with cheap first/last access. Both always accept new elements.
cards.example:
java.util.Queue a = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();      // ArrayDeque
java.util.Deque b = new java.util.LinkedList<>();         // LinkedList
java.util.Queue c = new java.util.PriorityQueue<>();      // PriorityQueue (Queue only)
System.out.println(a.getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + b.getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + c.getClass().getSimpleName());

cards.front: How does PriorityQueue decide which element is at its head?
cards.back: The least element according to natural order or the supplied Comparator
cards.extra: It is a heap, so iteration order is not sorted; only the head is guaranteed. Elements must be Comparable unless a comparator is given.
cards.example:
java.util.PriorityQueue natural = new java.util.PriorityQueue<>();
java.util.PriorityQueue reversed = new java.util.PriorityQueue<>(java.util.Comparator.reverseOrder());
natural.add(3); natural.add(1); reversed.add(3); reversed.add(1);
System.out.println(natural.peek() + " " + reversed.peek());   // 1 and 3: least by natural order or Comparator

cards.front: What happens if you insert a non-Comparable object into a PriorityQueue with no comparator?
cards.back: A ClassCastException at insertion time
cards.extra: The heap needs to compare the new element with existing ones to sift it into place, and fails immediately if it cannot.
cards.example: java.util.PriorityQueue

cards.front: Why should you avoid the legacy Stack class?
cards.back: It extends Vector, is synchronized on every call, and is legacy - use ArrayDeque
cards.extra: Vector is thread safe but discouraged, and Stack inherits that cost even when no thread safety is needed. For a thread-safe stack use BlockingDeque implementations.
cards.example:
java.util.Stack old = new java.util.Stack<>();
System.out.println(old instanceof java.util.Vector);   // true: legacy Stack extends Vector
java.util.Deque useThis = new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();   // not the synchronized legacy class
old.push("x"); useThis.push("x"); System.out.println(old.pop() + " " + useThis.pop());

cards.front: Which interfaces extend the Collections Framework into concurrent queue programming?
cards.back: BlockingQueue, BlockingDeque and TransferQueue
cards.extra: They live at the intersection of Collections and concurrency: blocking variants wait when a queue is full or empty instead of throwing or returning null.
cards.example:
java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue bq = new java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1);
java.util.concurrent.BlockingDeque bd = new java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingDeque<>();
java.util.concurrent.TransferQueue tq = new java.util.concurrent.LinkedTransferQueue<>();
System.out.println(bq.getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + bd.getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + tq.getClass().getSimpleName());

cards.front: Why prefer a for-each over an explicit Iterator loop?
cards.back: for-each is shorter but cannot remove; use an Iterator to delete while iterating
cards.extra: For plain reading, for-each is the option that hides the cursor entirely and cannot go wrong. Removal is the one job it does not support.
cards.example:
java.util.List list = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of("a", "b"));
for (String s : list) System.out.println(s);   // shorter, but cannot remove here
java.util.Iterator it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) if (it.next().equals("a")) it.remove();   // delete while iterating
System.out.println(list);   // [b]

cards.front: Which interface declares iterator(), and which interface extends it?
cards.back: Iterable declares it; Collection extends Iterable
cards.extra: That is why every collection in the hierarchy, and any class you write that implements Iterable, can be used in a for-each statement.
cards.example:
java.util.List list = java.util.List.of("a");
Iterable asIterable = list;   // Collection extends Iterable
java.util.Iterator it = asIterable.iterator();   // iterator() declared by Iterable
System.out.println(it.next());

cards.front: What is the correct two-step loop body when using an Iterator?
cards.back: Call hasNext() to test, then next() to advance
cards.extra: hasNext() is optional but protects you: calling next() with no elements left throws NoSuchElementException.
cards.example:
java.util.Iterator it = java.util.List.of("a", "b").iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) { String s = it.next(); System.out.println(s); }   // test, then advance

cards.front: What does Iterator.remove() delete?
cards.back: The element the last next() returned, once per next()
cards.extra: It is the only safe way to delete during an iteration; calling it twice in a row, or before any next(), throws IllegalStateException.
cards.example:
java.util.List list = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of("a", "b"));
java.util.Iterator it = list.iterator();
System.out.println(it.next()); it.remove();   // deletes what next() just returned: a
try { it.remove(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("once per next()"); }
System.out.println(list);   // [b]

cards.front: On which collections does Iterator.remove() throw UnsupportedOperationException?
cards.back: Immutable collections, such as those from List.of()
cards.extra: The ArrayList, LinkedList and HashSet iterators all support remove; factories returning unmodifiable collections cannot, since their collections have no remove at all.
cards.example:
java.util.Iterator it = java.util.List.of("a", "b").iterator();
it.next();
try { it.remove(); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("immutable collection: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }

cards.front: What is thrown when you modify a collection while iterating over it with a for-each or an Iterator?
cards.back: ConcurrentModificationException
cards.extra: Despite the name this is not about threads: a single-threaded structural modification during iteration triggers the fail-fast iterator.
cards.example:
java.util.List list = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of("a", "b"));
try { for (String s : list) { if (s.equals("a")) list.remove(s); } }
catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException e) { System.out.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }

cards.front: Which method removes matching elements from a collection while iterating, safely?
cards.back: removeIf(Predicate)
cards.extra: It hides the iterator handling and cannot produce a ConcurrentModificationException, unlike a hand-written loop that calls remove() on the collection.
cards.example:
java.util.List list = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of("keep", "drop", "keep"));
list.removeIf(s -> s.equals("drop"));   // removeIf(Predicate), safe while iterating
System.out.println(list);   // [keep, keep]

cards.text: A class works in a for-each as soon as it implements {{c1::Iterable}}, whose method {{c2::iterator()}} returns an {{c3::Iterator}}.
cards.extra: The generic parameter of Iterator is the element type, so Range implements Iterable<Integer> and its iterator() returns Iterator<Integer>.
cards.example:
class Ex {
    static class Bag implements Iterable {
        public java.util.Iterator iterator() { return java.util.List.of("x").iterator(); }
    }
    static void m() { for (String s : new Bag()) System.out.println(s); }   // for-each works
}

cards.front: What does a type parameter let you do that a formal parameter cannot?
cards.back: Pass a type instead of a value, so one implementation works for many types
cards.extra: Formal parameters take values, type parameters take types. That single distinction is what makes a class like Box<T> reusable and type-checked.

cards.front: Which two concrete benefits does generic code give over Object-based code?
cards.back: Compile-time type checking instead of runtime errors, and no casts
cards.extra: With Object-returning APIs, a wrong insertion is only discovered at runtime; generics catch it at compile time, and the compiler inserts the casts it knows are safe.
cards.example:
java.util.List names = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
names.add("Ada");
String first = names.get(0);   // checked at compile time, no cast
// names.add(42);              // caught now, not as a runtime ClassCastException
System.out.println(first);

cards.front: Match the conventional type parameter letters E, K, V, T to their meaning.
cards.back: E Element, K Key, V Value, T Type
cards.extra: Also N for Number and S, U, V for 2nd, 3rd, 4th types. Single uppercase letters keep a type variable visually distinct from a real class name.
cards.example:
class Holder { E e; }                 // E = Element
class Keyed { K k; V v; }          // K = Key, V = Value
class Wrapper { T t; }                // T = Type
class Ex { static void m() {
  System.out.println(Holder.class.getSimpleName() + " " + Keyed.class.getSimpleName() + " " + Wrapper.class.getSimpleName());
}}

cards.front: What may a type variable be substituted with?
cards.back: Any non-primitive type: class, interface, array, or another type variable
cards.extra: Primitives are excluded, which is why Box<int> does not compile; autoboxing happens at the call site instead, not in the type argument.

cards.front: What is the difference between a type parameter and a type argument?
cards.back: The parameter is T in Foo<T>; the argument is String in Foo<String>
cards.extra: You supply type arguments to build a parameterized type. Developers often say one for the other, but the definition is the declaration versus the usage.

cards.front: What is Box<Integer> called?
cards.back: A parameterized type - an invocation of a generic type
cards.extra: Reading it aloud is "Box of Integer". It is a type, not an object, so the statement still waits for a new before anything exists.

cards.front: What is <> called in new Box<>(), and since which release is it allowed?
cards.back: The diamond, allowed since Java SE 7
cards.extra: It replaces the type arguments in the constructor call when the compiler can infer them from the declaration on the left-hand side.
cards.example:
java.util.List names = new java.util.ArrayList<>();   // <> is the diamond (Java SE 7+)
names.add("Ada");
System.out.println(names);

cards.front: What is a raw type?
cards.back: A generic class or interface named without type arguments, such as Box
cards.extra: Raw types give pre-generics behaviour, so a raw Box hands back Object. A plain non-generic class is not a raw type.

cards.front: Why do raw types produce an unchecked warning rather than an error?
cards.back: They bypass generic checks and defer the failure to runtime
cards.extra: Assigning a parameterized type to its raw type is legal for compatibility; the reverse direction, and calling generic methods through a raw type, both warn.

cards.front: Which compiler flag shows the full detail of unchecked warnings?
cards.back: -Xlint:unchecked
cards.extra: Unchecked warnings are off by default with only a hint. The inverse, -Xlint:-unchecked, disables them; @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") silences a single site.

cards.front: Where do the type parameters go in a generic method declaration?
cards.back: Before the return type, as in <T> T first(List<T> l)
cards.extra: Their scope is limited to that method, unlike a class type parameter. Constructors may be generic too, with the same bracket placement.
cards.example:
class Ex {
    static  T first(java.util.List l) { return l.isEmpty() ? null : l.get(0); }
    static void m() { System.out.println(first(java.util.List.of(1, 2))); }
}

cards.front: Which method of a bounded type parameter makes The isEven()-style body possible on <T extends Number>?
cards.back: Any method declared on the bound, e.g. intValue() from Number
cards.extra: The bound both restricts the argument types and exposes the bound's API inside the body. Without it the variable has only Object's methods.

cards.front: In a multi-bound declaration <T extends A & B>, what happens if A is a class but is not written first?
cards.back: Compile-time error - the class must come before the interfaces
cards.extra: The type variable is a subtype of every bound, so only one class bound is possible and Java requires it to lead the list.

cards.front: <T extends Number>: does extends mean class extension only?
cards.back: No - it means extends or implements, depending on the bound
cards.extra: Bounds are written with one keyword for both cases, so <T extends Comparable<T>> happily accepts a class implementing the interface.

cards.front: Is Box<Integer> a subtype of Box<Number>?
cards.back: No - generic types are invariant
cards.extra: For any two distinct concrete types A and B, MyClass<A> and MyClass<B> are unrelated; their only common parent is Object.
cards.example:
class Box { T value; }
class Ex { static void m() {
  Box ints = new Box<>();
  // Box nums = ints;   // error: generic types are invariant, no subtyping
  Object any = ints;            // only a widening to Object works
}}

cards.front: What is the common supertype of List<Integer> and List<Number>?
cards.back: List<?> (with Object and raw List above it)
cards.extra: Not List<Object>: that is a concrete parameterization and is unrelated to a list of Integer. The unbounded wildcard is the meeting point.
cards.example:
java.util.List ints = java.util.List.of(1);
java.util.List nums = java.util.List.of(2.0);
java.util.List common = ints;   // also accepts nums: the common supertype
common = nums; Object obj = common; java.util.List raw = common;   // Object and raw List above it
System.out.println(obj + " " + raw);

cards.front: When is subtyping preserved between parameterized generic types?
cards.back: Only when the type argument is left unchanged
cards.extra: ArrayList<String> is a subtype of List<String>, which is a subtype of Collection<String>, all following the same declaration chain.

cards.front: Can a generic type be instantiated with a primitive type argument?
cards.back: No - only reference types: Pair<Integer, Character>, never Pair<int, char>
cards.extra: Autoboxing happens at the call site, not in the type argument, so the literal 8 becomes Integer.valueOf(8) while the declared type stays a wrapper.
cards.example:
class Pair { A a; B b; }
class Ex { static void m() {
  Pair ok = new Pair<>();   // reference types only
  // Pair bad = new Pair<>();        // error: primitives cannot be type arguments
}}

cards.front: Can you write new T() inside a generic class?
cards.back: No - compile-time error; use reflection instead
cards.extra: After erasure T may only exist as its bound or Object, so the compiler has no constructor to call. Reflection with a Class<T> token is the workaround.

cards.front: Why can't a class declare a static field of type T?
cards.back: A static field is shared by all parameterizations, so T would have no single value
cards.extra: If it were allowed, one field would have to be the T of every instance type at once. Static methods may still be generic, but with their own type parameter.

cards.front: What can the compiler check in place of a cast or an instanceof with a parameterized type?
cards.back: Only the unbounded wildcard form, e.g. o instanceof List<?>
cards.extra: At runtime the type arguments are gone, so instanceof List<String> and instanceof List<Integer> are indistinguishable.

cards.front: Why is new List<String>[10] rejected?
cards.back: Arrays are covariant and reified; parameterized types are neither
cards.extra: An array's store check must be able to throw ArrayStoreException. With erasure it cannot distinguish a List<String> from a List<Integer>, so it would silently admit the wrong element.
cards.example:
// java.util.List[] a = new java.util.List[10];   // error: generic array creation
java.util.List[] raw = new java.util.List[10];   // raw array, reified at runtime
Object[] covariant = raw;                        // arrays are covariant
raw[0] = java.util.List.of(1);
System.out.println(raw[0]);

cards.front: Can a generic class extend Throwable?
cards.back: No - not directly, not indirectly, not even as a type parameter
cards.extra: A catch clause must know the concrete type to dispatch, and overriding or catching a parameterized throwable would be erased to allow arbitrary subclasses.
cards.example:
class Boom extends Exception { }             // non-generic: allowed
// class Gen extends Exception { }          // error: generic class cannot extend Throwable
// class Indirect extends Boom { }          // error: not even indirectly
class Ex { static void m() { System.out.println(new Boom()); }}

cards.front: Can a method catch a value of a type parameter, as in catch (T e)?
cards.back: No - but a type parameter may appear in a throws clause
cards.extra: Catching needs the runtime class to match, which erasure destroys. Declaring void m() throws T is fine because the throws clause is only checked at compile time.

cards.front: Why can't void m(List<String> l) and void m(List<Integer> l) be overloaded?
cards.back: Both erase to the same signature m(List) - a name clash
cards.extra: Overloading is resolved on the erased signature stored in the class file, so the two overloads collide and the class does not compile.

cards.front: What does the compiler replace a type parameter with during erasure?
cards.back: Its first bound, or Object if it is unbounded
cards.extra: So Node<T> with T unbounded becomes a class with Object fields, and <T extends Comparable> becomes fields of type Comparable.

cards.front: What guarantee makes generics free at runtime?
cards.back: No new classes are created per parameterization, so there is no runtime overhead
cards.extra: The erased bytecode contains only ordinary classes and methods. The price is that type information is unavailable at runtime, which drives the restrictions.

cards.front: Besides substitution, what two things does erasure add to the bytecode?
cards.back: Required casts, and synthetic bridge methods
cards.extra: Casts restore type safety at the use site, and bridge methods restore polymorphism in subclasses that override with a concrete type.

cards.front: Why is a bridge method needed in a class extending a generic one?
cards.back: The erased overriding signature no longer matches the erased supertype method
cards.extra: Erasure turns Node.setData(T) into setData(Object), so MyNode.setData(Integer) would not override it. The compiler emits setData(Object) that casts and delegates.

cards.front: What exception does the bridge method produce after erasure when a wrong type reaches it?
cards.back: ClassCastException, thrown by the cast inside the bridge
cards.extra: The call is dispatched to the bridge, which casts the argument to the overridden type; the compiler's inserted cast is where the runtime check finally happens.

cards.front: What is a reifiable type?
cards.back: One whose type information is fully available at runtime
cards.extra: Primitives, non-generic types, raw types and unbounded wildcard invocations qualify. List<?> and List are reifiable; List<String> is not.

cards.front: What is a non-reifiable type?
cards.back: A parameterized type whose arguments are erased, e.g. List<String>
cards.extra: It has only partial runtime information, so it cannot be used in instanceof or as an array element; the JVM sees it as plain List.
cards.example:
java.util.List strings = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
Class runtime = strings.getClass();   // type argument erased at runtime
System.out.println(runtime);              // class java.util.ArrayList, no String in it
// if (strings instanceof java.util.List) {}   // error: non-reifiable type

cards.front: Define heap pollution.
cards.back: A variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that type
cards.extra: It follows from an unchecked operation: a raw-typed reference, an unchecked cast, or a varargs array. Code that compiles without warnings cannot pollute the heap.

cards.front: Why is T... elements dangerous in a generic method?
cards.back: Erasure rewrites the varargs parameter to Object[], which accepts any element type
cards.extra: The array of a parameterized type cannot legally be created, so the compiler builds an Object[] instead and type safety is lost through that hole.

cards.front: Which annotation asserts that a varargs method is safe against heap pollution?
cards.back: @SafeVarargs, on static, final and constructor declarations
cards.extra: It is part of the method's contract: a promise that the body does not mishandle the array. @SuppressWarnings silences only the declaration, not the call sites.
cards.example:
class Safe {
  @SafeVarargs static  java.util.List of(T... items) { return java.util.List.of(items); }
  @SafeVarargs final java.util.List list(String... s) { return java.util.List.of(s); }
  @SafeVarargs Safe(String... s) { }
}
class Ex { static void m() { System.out.println(Safe.of("a", "b")); }}

cards.front: What does the compiler use to infer type arguments for a generic method?
cards.back: The argument types, the target type, and possibly the expected return type
cards.extra: It then picks the most specific type that makes the invocation applicable - for example Serializable when it is the tightest common supertype of two arguments.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static  T id(T x) { return x; }
  static void m() {
    String byArg = id("s"); java.util.List byTarget = java.util.List.of();
    Number byReturn = id(Integer.valueOf(1));   // expected return type can also guide inference
  }
}

cards.front: What is a type witness, and when do you need one?
cards.back: Util.<Integer>compare(...) - an explicit type argument between dot and method name
cards.extra: Needed only when inference cannot succeed from the arguments and the target. Usually it can, so a generic method is called exactly like an ordinary one.
cards.example:
class Util {
  static > int compare(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b); }
}
class Ex { static void m() {
  System.out.println(Util.compare(1, 2));   // explicit type argument: the witness
}}

cards.front: Why must you write the diamond to get inference when instantiating a generic class?
cards.back: No diamond: it falls back to the raw type and warns about unchecked conversion
cards.extra: The constructor of a raw type refers to the raw class, not to Map<String, List<String>>, so assigning the result to that type becomes an unchecked operation.
cards.example:
java.util.List inferred = new java.util.ArrayList<>();   // diamond: T inferred
java.util.List raw = new java.util.ArrayList();                   // no diamond: raw type
java.util.List convert = raw;                             // unchecked conversion
System.out.println(inferred + " " + convert);

cards.front: Can a non-generic class have a generic constructor?
cards.back: Yes - constructors may declare their own type parameters
cards.extra: In new MyClass<Integer>("hi"), Integer is the class parameter X and String is inferred for the constructor parameter T.

cards.front: Since which Java release can the diamond infer the type of the class being instantiated?
cards.back: Java SE 7
cards.extra: Before 7, compilers could infer generic constructor parameters but not the class's own type arguments; with the diamond the target type of the assignment drives the choice.

cards.front: What is the target type of an expression?
cards.back: The type the compiler expects where the expression sits
cards.extra: In List<String> l = Collections.emptyList(); the target type is List<String>, so T is inferred as String with no witness needed.
cards.example:
CharSequence cs = "hello";   // target type: compiler expects CharSequence here
String s = "hello";          // same expression with String as target type
System.out.println(cs.length() + " " + s.length());

cards.front: In Java SE 7, why did processStringList(Collections.emptyList()) fail to compile?
cards.back: Method arguments were not yet target types, so T defaulted to Object
cards.extra: Java SE 8 widened target typing to include method arguments and lambda bodies, so the same call now compiles and T becomes String.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static void processStringList(java.util.List l) { }
  static void m() {
    processStringList(java.util.Collections.emptyList());   // target type infers String in Java 8+
    // Java SE 7: arguments were not target types, T defaulted to Object, so this failed to compile
  }
}

cards.front: How is the type of a lambda expression determined?
cards.back: From the target type of the context - the functional interface expected there
cards.extra: That is why a lambda needs an interface in scope: the same () -> "done" is Runnable in one context and Callable in another.
cards.example:
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("run");   // target type: Runnable
java.util.function.IntUnaryOperator f = x -> x + 1;   // target type decides parameter and result
r.run(); System.out.println(f.applyAsInt(2));

cards.front: Name the contexts in which a lambda can legally appear.
cards.back: Variable declarations, assignments, returns, array initializers, arguments, casts
cards.extra: These are the eight target-typed positions: also lambda bodies, conditional expressions and method or constructor arguments. Each supplies the functional interface to implement.

cards.front: Which of two overloads does invoke(() -> "done") pick, invoke(Runnable) or invoke(Callable<T>)?
cards.back: invoke(Callable<T>) - a lambda returning a value is not void-compatible
cards.extra: Overload resolution plus target typing eliminate the void alternative because the body produces a value, so the Callable overload is the only applicable one.

cards.front: What does List<? extends Number> accept that List<Number> does not?
cards.back: Lists of subtypes: List<Integer>, List<Double>, and any other Number subclass
cards.extra: The plain parameterization matches exactly one type; the upper-bounded wildcard matches that type and everything below it, which is what makes reusable methods possible.

cards.front: Inside a method taking List<? extends Foo>, how may you read elements and may you add?
cards.back: Read them as Foo; adding is rejected except for null
cards.extra: The compiler only knows the list is some subtype of Foo, and cannot confirm that your Foo is that subtype. So the type is effectively read-only.

cards.front: Which two situations call for an unbounded wildcard <?>?
cards.back: You only use Object methods, or the methods you use do not depend on the type parameter
cards.extra: The second is why Class<?> is so common: most of Class's API ignores T. null is the only value you can add to a List<?>.

cards.front: How do List<Object> and List<?> differ for adding?
cards.back: List<Object> takes any Object; List<?> takes only null
cards.extra: They are not the same type. List<?> is a list of unknown type, so no value can be proven compatible; List<Object> is known to accept Object and its subtypes.
cards.example: java.util.List

cards.front: What does the lower-bounded wildcard List<? super Integer> match?
cards.back: Integer and all its supertypes - Integer, Number, Object
cards.extra: Its job is writing: any of those lists can hold an Integer. Symmetric to the upper bound, which enables reading.

cards.front: Can a wildcard have both an upper and a lower bound?
cards.back: No - ? extends X or ? super X, never both
cards.extra: A bound is a one-directional constraint on the unknown type; there is no syntax for an interval. Bounds are also only for wildcards, not for type parameters.

cards.front: Why is List<Integer> not a subtype of List<Number>?
cards.back: Generics are invariant: subtyping follows only the declaration chain
cards.extra: ArrayList<E> implements List<E> so ArrayList<String> is a List<String>, but a change of type argument breaks the relationship entirely - these two are unrelated apart from Object and List<?>.

cards.front: What is the common parent of List<Number> and List<Integer>?
cards.back: List<?>
cards.extra: That is the joining point wildcards provide. List<? extends Number> then sits between it and List<Number> in the type hierarchy.
cards.example:
java.util.List nums = java.util.List.of(1.0);
java.util.List ints = java.util.List.of(1);
java.util.List both = nums; both = ints;   // List is their common parent
System.out.println(both);

cards.front: What does the compiler report when it says "capture of ?"?
cards.back: It inferred a hidden type variable for a wildcard and cannot prove your write is safe
cards.extra: Wildcard capture is usually invisible. A private helper method named fooHelper(...) gives the captured type a name, letting the compiler accept a safe call.

cards.front: State the PECS guideline: which wildcard for an "in" variable and which for an "out" variable?
cards.back: in: ? extends; out: ? super
cards.extra: Mnemonic Producer Extends, Consumer Super: data you read from is produced by the parameter, data you write into is consumed by it. Use no wildcard when both happen.

cards.front: Should a return type use a wildcard?
cards.back: No - it forces every caller to deal with the wildcard
cards.extra: The guidelines apply to parameters, not results. Returning List<? extends Foo> takes away the caller's freedom for no benefit they asked for.

cards.front: On a List<? extends NaturalNumber>, which four operations are still allowed?
cards.back: Add null, clear(), iterate and remove(), write back read elements
cards.extra: So it is not strictly read-only, but you cannot add or change elements through it: no new value can be proven to be of the unknown subtype.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: Name the three elements every pattern matching operation has.
cards.back: The matched target, the pattern, and the result of the match
cards.extra: Even with a regex these hold: the sonnet is the target, \bflame\b is the pattern, the start and end indexes are the result.

cards.front: In which Java release did pattern matching for instanceof become final?
cards.back: Java SE 16
cards.extra: Before 16 you checked the type and then declared a local variable to cast; afterwards the cast is folded into the pattern o instanceof String s.

cards.front: What is a pattern variable?
cards.back: The variable declared inside the pattern, bound only if the match succeeded
cards.extra: In o instanceof String s, s is created with the type String only when o really is a String. A pattern may declare several pattern variables.

cards.front: What is a type pattern?
cards.back: A type followed by a variable declaration, used as the right operand of instanceof
cards.extra: It checks the type of the matched target and binds the variable. The type may be a class, an abstract class or an interface, so CharSequence matches a String.

cards.front: Where may a pattern variable be used, besides the if body?
cards.back: Also the boolean expression after &&, which only runs if the match succeeded
cards.extra: Short-circuit evaluation guarantees the variable exists there. The right side of || does not qualify, since it can run when the match failed.

cards.front: When can a pattern variable be used after the if statement?
cards.back: Only when the if branch cannot fall through - it returns or throws
cards.extra: If the branch can continue into the rest of the method, the compiler cannot prove the match happened and refuses the use outside.

cards.front: Why does pi instanceof String s fail to compile when pi is a Point?
cards.back: The compiler knows String is final, so the match can never succeed
cards.extra: A statically impossible pattern is an error rather than dead code. Sealed and final types give the compiler enough information to reject it.

cards.front: In which release did pattern matching for switch become final?
cards.back: JDK 21, after previews in 17 through 20
cards.extra: It allows type patterns as case labels, so a chain of if (o instanceof ...) tests collapses into one switch expression.

cards.front: Which types does switch accept as case labels, before type patterns are added?
cards.back: byte, short, char, int, their wrappers, String, and enums
cards.extra: long is not in the list, and neither are float, double or boolean. Pattern matching for switch adds type patterns to that set.

cards.front: What is a guarded case label?
cards.back: A type pattern followed by a boolean expression in a when clause
cards.extra: Example: case String s when !s.isEmpty(). The guard is needed because a case label cannot itself be a boolean expression.

cards.front: Why can't you write case s.isEmpty(): in a switch?
cards.back: Case labels must be constant expressions, and a boolean test is not one
cards.extra: The guard clause when exists precisely to express a condition alongside a type pattern, since case labels cannot be booleans.

cards.front: What is record deconstruction in a record pattern?
cards.back: A record pattern that declares one pattern per component, binding each from the accessor
cards.extra: o instanceof Point(int x, int y) calls x() and y(). That matters: accessors may return defensive copies.

cards.front: Which constructor's shape must a record pattern follow?
cards.back: The canonical constructor, regardless of the other constructors declared
cards.extra: Extra constructors do not affect pattern syntax; a pattern written to match a non-canonical constructor does not compile.

cards.front: In a record pattern, may a component pattern use var?
cards.back: Yes - the component's real type is inferred
cards.extra: You may also widen it to a supertype of the component's type. Naming a type that the component could not possibly be extended to is a compile error.

cards.front: Do record patterns support boxing and unboxing?
cards.back: No - a component pattern's type must match or be a supertype, without conversion
cards.extra: So a pattern expecting Integer against an int component fails, and the reverse too. Nesting record patterns, however, is supported.

cards.front: Which three language constructs support pattern matching, and which two kinds of patterns?
cards.back: instanceof, switch, and the extended for loop; type patterns and record patterns
cards.extra: All three accept the same two pattern kinds, so the mental model learned for one transfers directly to the others.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::02 High Order Functions

cards.front: What do the default methods of the java.util.function interfaces enable?
cards.back: Combining and chaining lambda expressions into one readable expression
cards.extra: They hide the technical complexity and expose the intent. They must be default, since only one abstract method is allowed on a functional interface.

cards.front: Which three methods combine two predicates?
cards.back: and(), or(), and negate()
cards.extra: and and or take another Predicate; negate takes nothing. Each returns a new Predicate rather than mutating the receiver.

cards.front: Which Predicate factory methods create a predicate from scratch?
cards.back: Predicate.isEqual(target), and its negation Predicate.not()
cards.extra: isEqual produces a test for equality with the given object; not() inverts a predicate passed as an argument. Both are static.

cards.front: Which method chains two Consumers so that both run, in order?
cards.back: c1.andThen(c2)
cards.extra: The first consumer receives the element, then the second. Used for patterns like logging and then printing the same value.

cards.front: How do f1.andThen(f2) and f2.compose(f1) differ in what they compute?
cards.back: Nothing - both give the same function; only the call site differs
cards.extra: andThen extends the first function, compose prepends its argument. You need to call andThen on f1 or compose on f2 to get the same result.

cards.front: What is the constraint when chaining functions of different types?
cards.back: The result type of f1 must be compatible with the input type of f2
cards.extra: Function<A, B>.andThen(Function<B, C>) yields Function<A, C>. The compiler enforces the middle type matches.

cards.front: Which factory method creates the identity function?
cards.back: Function.identity()
cards.extra: It returns its own argument unchanged, and it is generic over any type. Common as a classifier in groupingBy, where the element is its own key.

cards.front: What three steps turn a lambda into code?
cards.back: Identify the type, find the abstract method, implement it
cards.extra: A lambda is an implementation of the single abstract method of a functional interface, so the work is mechanical once you know which interface applies.

cards.front: What type must a lambda expression have?
cards.back: A functional interface - an interface with exactly one abstract method
cards.extra: An anonymous class that does not implement a functional interface cannot be rewritten as a lambda, because there would be no single method to implement.

cards.front: Do concrete interface methods count against a functional interface's single abstract method?
cards.back: No - default and static methods are concrete and do not count
cards.extra: Predicate is functional with three default and two static methods, because it has just one abstract method (test).

cards.front: Is @FunctionalInterface required on a functional interface?
cards.back: No - it is an optional check that errors on a type with the wrong shape
cards.extra: Interfaces written before Java SE 8 became functional without modification, so the annotation cannot be a requirement. It documents intent and protects against edits.

cards.front: What are the three syntactic elements of a lambda expression?
cards.back: A parameter block, the arrow ->, and a body
cards.extra: Java uses the thin arrow ->, not the fat arrow =>. The parameter block mirrors the abstract method's signature.

cards.front: Which two simplifications does the compiler allow in a lambda's parameter list?
cards.back: Drop the parameter types, and drop the parentheses when there is exactly one parameter
cards.extra: So (String s) -> ... becomes s -> .... Parentheses are required for zero parameters, as in () -> ....

cards.front: When can a lambda body omit braces and return?
cards.back: When the body is a single expression
cards.extra: A multi-statement body needs braces, and once braces are used a value-returning body must use an explicit return.

cards.front: Can a lambda override a default method of its interface?
cards.back: No - a lambda implements only the abstract method
cards.extra: Calling the abstract method runs your lambda code; calling a default method runs the interface's code. There is no syntax to replace the latter.

cards.front: What compile error appears when a lambda mutates a captured local variable?
cards.back: "Variable used in lambda expression should be final or effectively final"
cards.extra: Lambdas capture values, not variables. A variable the lambda only reads without reassigning is called effectively final and is accepted.

cards.front: What is an effectively final variable?
cards.back: One never reassigned after initialization, so the compiler treats it as final
cards.extra: Java SE 8 introduced the notion so lambdas can capture ordinary locals. The compiler does not add final to your source, only relies on it.

cards.front: Can lambda expressions be serialized?
cards.back: Yes - lambdas were built to be serializable
cards.extra: Needed because a lambda can end up in a field of an object and therefore in its serialized state, which must stay compatible with existing serializable classes.

cards.front: How many interfaces does java.util.function contain, roughly, and around what are they organized?
cards.back: Over 40, organized around the four main shapes
cards.extra: Supplier, Consumer, Predicate and Function. Learn those four and the rest read as variants: bivariants, primitive specializations, operators.

cards.front: State the input and output of the four core functional shapes.
cards.back: Supplier: nothing in, T. Consumer: T in, void. Predicate: T in, boolean. Function: T in, R
cards.extra: Every other interface in the package is one of these four with a second argument, a primitive type, or both. The four also map to supplier/consumer in stream pipelines.

cards.front: Which is the only abstract method of Supplier<T>?
cards.back: T get()
cards.extra: The interface has no default or static methods at all. A supplier called repeatedly may return a new object every time, such as a random integer.

cards.front: Which single method does Consumer<T> declare as abstract, and what does Iterable.forEach take?
cards.back: void accept(T t); forEach(Consumer<? super T>)
cards.extra: Practical consequences: list.forEach(System.out::println) prints every element, and forEach is the standard internal iteration hook.

cards.front: Which method do all specialized primitive consumers share?
cards.back: accept, e.g. void accept(int value) in IntConsumer
cards.extra: Consumers are named after the type they take: IntConsumer, LongConsumer, DoubleConsumer. With a void return there is only one name to use.

cards.front: Which four specialized Supplier interfaces avoid boxing?
cards.back: IntSupplier, LongSupplier, DoubleSupplier, BooleanSupplier
cards.extra: Their method names add the return type to get: getAsInt(), getAsLong(), getAsDouble(), getAsBoolean(). No wrapper object is created per call.

cards.front: What naming rule do all primitive-returning functional method names follow?
cards.back: get or apply plus the returned type, e.g. applyAsInt()
cards.extra: The base method name (get, apply) gains an AsX suffix. Therefore IntSupplier has getAsInt and ToIntFunction has applyAsInt.

cards.front: What is the difference between BiConsumer<T, U> and Consumer<T>?
cards.back: BiConsumer takes two arguments and returns nothing
cards.extra: Specializations exist as ObjIntConsumer, ObjLongConsumer and ObjDoubleConsumer - exactly one of the two arguments is a primitive.

cards.front: Is there a primitive-specialized BiPredicate?
cards.back: No - BiPredicate has no primitive variants
cards.extra: Bipredicates follow the same bivariant convention as consumers and functions, but the JDK did not add IntBiPredicate and its siblings.

cards.front: Which collection method takes a predicate and removes matching elements?
cards.back: removeIf(Predicate<? super E>)
cards.extra: It mutates the collection, so calling it on List.of() results or on a List from Arrays.asList() throws an exception.

cards.front: Which interfaces extend Function<T, R> for same-type transformations, and what do they model?
cards.back: UnaryOperator<T> and BinaryOperator<T>
cards.extra: UnaryOperator takes and returns the same T, BinaryOperator takes two and returns one. Math operations like sqrt or addition are the classic examples.

cards.front: Which method applies a UnaryOperator to every element of a list?
cards.back: list.replaceAll(unaryOperator)
cards.extra: Only element values change, never their types - a reason the JDK chose UnaryOperator over Function: a List<String> must stay a List<String>.

cards.front: What is the difference between Function and BiFunction?
cards.back: BiFunction<T, U, R> takes two inputs and returns R
cards.extra: Its abstract method is R apply(T t, U u). Specialized forms exist as IntBinaryOperator and ToIntBiFunction<T> style interfaces.

cards.front: Since when does Iterable.forEach let you iterate without an explicit loop?
cards.back: Java SE 8, as part of the Collections/lambda update
cards.extra: It performs internal iteration: the collection advances itself and you supply only the action, which is more readable than an index or iterator loop.

cards.front: When can a lambda expression be replaced by a method reference?
cards.back: When its body is just a call to an existing method, with arguments passed straight through
cards.extra: The reference names the method instead of describing the forwarding. IDs like System.out::println are the same lambda with the noise removed.

cards.front: List the four kinds of method references with their syntax.
cards.back: Static Type::staticMethod, bound obj::method, unbound Type::method, Type::new
cards.extra: All four are :: expressions; what differs is whether the receiver is a type, an expression, or absent (constructor).

cards.front: What distinguishes a bound from an unbound method reference?
cards.back: Bound fixes the receiver in the reference; unbound takes it as the first argument
cards.extra: System.out::println is bound to the object System.out. User::getName is unbound: the User is passed when the lambda is invoked.

cards.front: What is String::length an unbound reference to, given that length() is an instance method?
cards.back: An unbound reference where the String is the argument
cards.extra: It reads like a static call but is not one: the lambda is s -> s.length(), which fits ToIntFunction<String>.

cards.front: What is the lambda equivalent of ArrayList::new?
cards.back: () -> new ArrayList<>()
cards.extra: The constructor reference picks a constructor from the functional interface's signature. Its target type decides which constructor overload is selected.

cards.front: Why is ArrayList::new ambiguous on its own?
cards.back: The target type determines which constructor is meant
cards.extra: As a Supplier<List<String>> it uses the no-arg constructor; as IntFunction<List<String>> it uses the capacity constructor. Same syntax, different behaviour.

cards.front: Can you write ArrayList<>::new?
cards.back: No - the diamond is not allowed there; give the full type or nothing
cards.extra: A constructor reference has no inference context to fill the diamond at that point, so either ArrayList::new or ArrayList<String>::new.

cards.front: Which single abstract method does Comparator<T> declare?
cards.back: int compare(T o1, T o2), which makes it a functional interface
cards.extra: Introduced back in JDK 2, it became implementable with a lambda only once functional interfaces existed in Java SE 8.

cards.front: State the contract of Comparator.compare in terms of sign.
cards.back: Negative if o1 < o2, positive if o1 > o2, and opposite signs for the swapped call
cards.extra: Returning 0 is not required when equals() is true. Break the contract and sorting behaviour becomes unspecified.

cards.front: Why is (i1, i2) -> i1 - i2 a bad comparator?
cards.back: Integer subtraction overflows for distant values, reversing the sign
cards.extra: So the comparison silently gives the wrong order for large ranges. Use Integer.compare(i1, i2), which is overflow-safe.

cards.front: Which method makes a comparator from a key extractor function?
cards.back: Comparator.comparing(Function)
cards.extra: The function must return a Comparable type. Comparator.comparing(User::getName) sorts users by name with no explicit comparison code.

cards.front: Which default method chains comparators as tie-breakers?
cards.back: thenComparing(Comparator), with a key-extractor overload
cards.extra: It runs the second comparator only when the first returns 0. thenComparing(User::getLastName) is the equivalent with a function.

cards.front: Which comparator factory sorts by a type's compareTo?
cards.back: Comparator.naturalOrder()
cards.extra: It compares any Comparable via compareTo. Its reverse is reverseOrder(), and it is the usual tie-breaker in chains.

cards.front: Which factory methods move nulls to the end or the start of the order?
cards.back: Comparator.nullsLast(cmp) and nullsFirst(cmp)
cards.extra: They wrap an existing comparator and handle nulls for you. Hand-rolling null checks inside compare is the main source of accidental NullPointerException.

cards.front: Which Comparator method inverts the ordering?
cards.back: reversed()
cards.extra: It returns a new comparator with the sign inverted, so it composes with comparing and thenComparing instead of duplicating the logic.

cards.front: Which List method sorts with a comparator?
cards.back: list.sort(comparator), added in Java SE 8
cards.extra: It replaces Collections.sort(list, cmp). Sorting in reverse is then list.sort(cmp.reversed()).

cards.front: Which comparator methods avoid boxing when comparing primitive keys?
cards.back: comparingInt, comparingLong, comparingDouble
cards.extra: They take a ToIntFunction, ToLongFunction or ToDoubleFunction instead of a Function, so no wrapper object is created per comparison.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::03 Functional Composition

cards.front: Which method turns a file into a Stream<String> of its lines?
cards.back: Files.lines(Path) from java.nio.file
cards.extra: It replaces the BufferedReader plus while-readLine loop with one call, and removes the boilerplate around reading each line.

cards.front: What does Files.lines() need besides a Path when the file is not UTF-8?
cards.back: An overload taking a Charset
cards.extra: UTF-8 is the default, so the two-argument form exists only for other encodings. The stream must be closed, so use it in try-with-resources.

cards.front: What does a file stream replace when iterating: an external or an internal iterator?
cards.back: External iteration becomes internal iteration
cards.extra: The buffered reader loop fetched one line at a time; the stream drives the traversal itself and you supply only the action on each line.

cards.front: How do you count the lines of a file that contain a word, in stream style?
cards.back: filter(line -> line.contains(word)).count()
cards.extra: The imperative if inside the read loop is exactly the filter stage, and count() is the terminal operation that consumes the result.

cards.front: How many terminal operations does a stream pipeline need to actually run?
cards.back: Exactly one, at the end
cards.extra: Without it a stream executes nothing. That is why the plain Files.lines(...).filter(...) lines appear to do nothing until count() or forEach() is added.

cards.front: What does a Java 5 for (String s : list) compile down to?
cards.back: A while loop over an Iterator
cards.extra: Foreach is syntax sugar: call hasNext(), fetch the next element, repeat. That makes the Iterable contract the foundation of the loop.

cards.front: Which method replaces a foreach loop in functional style?
cards.back: forEach(Consumer) on the collection or stream
cards.extra: The loop body becomes a lambda receiving each element. Called an internal iterator, because advancing is handled by the API, not your code.

cards.front: Where is forEach available: on Collection, on Stream, or both?
cards.back: Both
cards.extra: filter and the other intermediate operations, by contrast, exist only on Stream and not on Collection, so that several stages can be optimized together before a terminal operation runs.

cards.front: Which stream method replaces the if inside a loop?
cards.back: filter(predicate)
cards.extra: It acts like a gate: true lets the element through to the next stage, false discards it. Replacing if alone, the count of elements can shrink.

cards.front: What does filter() return?
cards.back: A new stream containing only the elements that passed the predicate
cards.extra: Nothing is processed yet; this is an intermediate operation, so filter only builds the pipeline until a terminal operation consumes it.

cards.front: Which stream method replaces a transformation inside a loop?
cards.back: map(function)
cards.extra: A loop that assigns the transformed value back to a variable is a map; the function models the transformation itself, not the iteration.

cards.front: How does map differ from filter in effect on the element count?
cards.back: map keeps the count and changes the type; filter keeps the type and reduces the count
cards.extra: Mapping is one-to-one, so ten elements remain ten. Filtering only removes elements, so the types cannot change.

cards.front: Where does map go in a pipeline that selects and then transforms?
cards.back: After filter
cards.extra: The filter discards unwanted elements and passes the rest; the map then transforms only what survived, saving work on the removed ones.

cards.front: What should you do first when a loop body does both transforming and printing?
cards.back: Split the loop body into two cohesive statements before refactoring
cards.extra: Mixed responsibilities make the map plus forEach sketch unreadable. Separating them exposes the transformation, which becomes the map stage.

cards.front: Which stream API form further shortens name -> name.toUpperCase()?
cards.back: A method reference: String::toUpperCase
cards.extra: When the lambda body is a single call on its own argument, the method reference names it without repeating the parameter.

cards.front: Which IntStream method replaces a for loop that skips values?
cards.back: iterate(seed, IntPredicate, IntUnaryOperator)
cards.extra: Seed is the first value, the predicate is the loop condition, and the operator is the increment. A filter() would waste work and still need the range.

cards.front: Map the three parts of for (int i = 0; i < 15; i += 3) onto Iterate's parameters.
cards.back: 0 seed, i < 15 as IntPredicate, i += 3 as IntUnaryOperator
cards.extra: The semicolons essentially turn into commas. Both conditions and increments become lambdas instead of loop clauses.

cards.front: Which method is the functional equivalent of break?
cards.back: takeWhile(predicate)
cards.extra: It terminates the stream when the predicate returns false. dropWhile is the opposite door: it skips elements until the predicate fails, then stays open.

cards.front: Can takeWhile let elements through again after it has stopped?
cards.back: No - once it closes, no further elements pass
cards.extra: It behaves like a one-way door. The same is true in reverse for dropWhile: once opened it never closes again.

cards.front: Which intStream.iterate overload turns an unbounded loop into an infinite stream?
cards.back: iterate(seed, IntUnaryOperator), with no predicate
cards.extra: Dropping the predicate leaves an endless source, which is then limited by takeWhile or limit. A stream must be bounded before a terminal operation collects it.

cards.front: Which stream methods require an ORDERED stream to make sense?
cards.back: takeWhile and dropWhile
cards.extra: Without an order there is no 'while' to reason about; on an unordered stream the downstream may receive any subset of the upstream elements.

cards.front: How do imperative and functional style differ in what they state?
cards.back: Imperative says what and how; functional says what and delegates the how
cards.extra: A for loop spells out index creation, increment and termination. A range based pipeline names only the interval and the action.

cards.front: Which IntStream method replaces for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)?
cards.back: IntStream.range(0, 5)
cards.extra: Both bounds behave as in the for loop: the start is included, and the end 5 is excluded, producing 0 to 4.

cards.front: Which method iterates up to and including the end value?
cards.back: IntStream.rangeClosed(0, 5)
cards.extra: The only difference from range is the inclusive end bound. Use rangeClosed whenever the loop condition is <=.

cards.front: What does IntStream.range return, and how do you print each value?
cards.back: An IntStream, consumed with forEach
cards.extra: A primitive stream has no forEachIndexed or index loop; the value arrives directly and can be printed with a method reference.

cards.front: What is the main structural benefit of the internal iterator over a for loop?
cards.back: The index and its mutation disappear; you supply only the per-element action
cards.extra: There is no counter to get wrong, so the code is shorter and easier to change. The same range pipeline can save to a database instead of printing.

cards.front: Which object carries a stream's characteristics, and what is its name derived from?
cards.back: The Spliterator - a contraction of split and iterator
cards.extra: It plays the iterator role in the Stream API and also decides how the data splits across CPUs. It is the source of all the stream characteristics.

cards.front: What do the characteristics ORDERED, SIZED, SORTED mean for a stream?
cards.back: ORDERED: order matters. SIZED: count is known. SORTED: already sorted
cards.extra: Two others in the tutorial are DISTINCT (no duplicates) and NONNULL (no nulls), plus SUBSIZED. Each is one bit in the Spliterator's characteristics word.

cards.front: What does SUBSIZED add on top of SIZED?
cards.back: Splitting produces two SIZED halves, so each half's size is known in advance
cards.extra: Essential for parallel streams: it lets the framework split work evenly without counting. An ArrayList is SUBSIZED, a HashSet is SIZED but not SUBSIZED.

cards.front: Which single method tests whether a stream has a characteristic?
cards.back: spliterator.hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.ORDERED)
cards.extra: It reads one bit of the word returned by characteristics(). Checking the bit by hand works too but is the unreadable option.

cards.front: Which intermediate method removes the ORDERED characteristic from a stream?
cards.back: unordered()
cards.extra: Keeping order can force coordination in a parallel stream, so dropping it is sometimes a deliberate optimization when order is irrelevant.

cards.front: Which characteristic is kept by map()/flatMap() when filtering would keep it?
cards.back: SORTED and DISTINCT survive filter, but are lost on map/flatMap
cards.extra: Removing elements cannot create duplicates or destroy the sort; transforming elements can change both, so those bits do not survive.

cards.front: Which stream operations erase SIZED and SUBSIZED?
cards.back: flatMap, filter, and distinct
cards.extra: The element count can no longer be predicted from the source. map and sorted preserve both; these three do not.

cards.front: Is a stream created from Files.lines(path) SIZED?
cards.back: No - you must read the file to know the number of lines
cards.extra: The byte size of the file does not equal the line count, so the framework cannot know the total without consuming the stream.

cards.front: Which collection stream is SIZED but not SUBSIZED, and why?
cards.back: HashSet - buckets can hold several elements, so halves are unequal
cards.extra: Splitting the bucket array in the middle does not guarantee equal element counts, so each half must be counted rather than computed.

cards.front: Name the three ways to build a custom collector.
cards.back: Combine collectors, use collect()'s three components, or implement Collector
cards.extra: Implementing Collector is the most flexible and the most technical option. Collectors factory methods with downstream collectors cover most needs.

cards.front: What does each of Collector<T, A, R>'s three type parameters mean?
cards.back: T stream element, A mutable intermediate container, R final result
cards.extra: For a toList-style collector, T is the element type, A is ArrayList<T> and R is List<T>. A may equal R, as in toSet.

cards.front: Why does an IDE show ? for the second type of a collector from the factory class?
cards.back: The factory methods hide A behind the declared return type
cards.extra: You cannot name ArrayList<T> there because the API does not expose it; only a hand-written Collector implementation must state A explicitly.

cards.front: What do the three collector characteristics IDENTITY_FINISH, UNORDERED, CONCURRENT mean?
cards.back: Finisher is identity; order is not preserved; the container supports concurrent access
cards.extra: They live in the Collector.Characteristics enum and are returned by characteristics(). toSet has UNORDERED; toList does not.

cards.front: Why is the IDENTITY_FINISH characteristic an optimization?
cards.back: The implementation can skip calling the finisher altogether
cards.extra: With no transformation between container and result, that step would be a no-op, so declaring it lets the stream runtime omit the call.

cards.front: Which characteristic of a collector only matters for parallel streams?
cards.back: CONCURRENT
cards.extra: It states that the accumulator container can be filled from several threads at once. Without it, parallel collection must merge per-thread containers afterwards.

cards.front: For a custom toList()-like collector, what are the supplier, accumulator and finisher?
cards.back: ArrayList::new, List::add, and the identity finisher
cards.extra: The container is already the result, so only IDENTITY_FINISH appears in the characteristics and no transformation runs at the end.

cards.front: For a toSet()-like collector, what is the one notable change from toList()?
cards.back: Supplier becomes HashSet::new, and UNORDERED is added
cards.extra: A set does not preserve insertion order, and that is exactly what the UNORDERED characteristic tells the runtime so it can optimize.

cards.front: Why is the joining() collector's characteristic set empty?
cards.back: It preserves order, has a real finisher, and does not support concurrent access
cards.extra: The container is a StringBuffer, finish is toString(), and order matters for concatenation. None of the three characteristics applies.

cards.front: Which four Stream factory methods create a stream from data you already hold?
cards.back: of(varargs), generate(supplier), iterate(seed, op), builder()
cards.extra: Stream.empty() makes a fifth, empty stream. of() delegates to Arrays.stream, so varargs and arrays behave the same.

cards.front: Why does Map have no stream() method, and what do you do instead?
cards.back: Stream a view: keySet(), entrySet() or values()
cards.extra: A map is not a Collection in the hierarchy, so it inherits nothing. entrySet is the usual choice when both key and value are needed.

cards.front: Which three arguments does the StreamSupport.stream(Spliterator, boolean) idiom for an iterator need from you?
cards.back: An estimate of size, characteristics, and a parallel flag
cards.extra: They wrap an Iterator in a spliterator so any non-standard source can become a stream. The size estimate may be Long.MAX_VALUE when unknown.

cards.front: Which method builds an infinite constant stream from a supplier?
cards.back: Stream.generate(supplier)
cards.extra: The supplier is called for each new element, forever. Always cut it with limit() or findFirst, or the process exhausts memory or hangs.

cards.front: What does limit(n) guarantee about a generate() stream?
cards.back: Generation stops after n elements - it is short-circuiting
cards.extra: Elements flow one at a time through all stages, so once the limit is satisfied no further supplier calls happen.

cards.front: Can an infinite stream be used without a terminal operation?
cards.back: No - a terminal operation both triggers and must bound the consumption
cards.extra: A stream does nothing without one, but adding one to an unbounded source must include limit, findFirst, or similar to halt the pipeline.

cards.front: How do Stream.generate and Stream.iterate differ?
cards.back: generate takes a supplier; iterate takes a seed plus a unary operator
cards.extra: generate needs no previous element, so every element is independent. iterate builds each value from the last, so the sequence is cumulative.

cards.front: What does the Java SE 9 overload of iterate add?
cards.back: A predicate that stops generation when it turns false
cards.extra: iterate(seed, hasNext, next) replaces the follow-up takeWhile and is the functional equivalent of a bounded for loop with a step.

cards.front: What is the difference between IntStream.range(a, b) and rangeClosed(a, b)?
cards.back: range excludes b; rangeClosed includes it
cards.extra: So LongStream.range(0L, 10L) produces 0 through 9. Both exist on IntStream and LongStream, neither on DoubleStream.

cards.front: Which method is needed to turn the int values of an IntStream.range into objects?
cards.back: mapToObj(i -> ...)
cards.extra: IntStream is a primitive stream, so mapping to a reference type needs mapToObj rather than map, which stays primitive.

cards.front: Which three Random methods produce a stream of random numbers?
cards.back: ints(), longs(), doubles()
cards.extra: Their bounds follow the usual convention: the lower bound is inclusive and the upper bound exclusive. All three are also overloaded with a stream size.

cards.front: Why would you seed a Random before streaming?
cards.back: A fixed seed gives a reproducible sequence, which makes tests deterministic
cards.extra: The same seed always yields the same numbers, so a test can assert on exact output. Unseeded, the sequence differs on every run.

cards.front: Which specialized stream method converts a primitive stream to its boxed wrapper stream?
cards.back: boxed()
cards.extra: An IntStream becomes a Stream<Integer>. The reverse direction uses mapToInt, and both are needed when the pipeline mixes primitives with objects.

cards.front: Which method gives the characters of a String as a stream, and as what type?
cards.back: String.chars(), returning an IntStream of code points
cards.extra: Each element is the numeric code point, not a char. To rebuild a one-character String use Character.toString(int) on Java SE 11 and later.

cards.front: Which method streams a file's lines with a charset overload, and how must the stream be closed?
cards.back: Files.lines(Path), closed with try-with-resources
cards.extra: Stream extends BaseStream which extends AutoCloseable, so the stream itself is a resource. For I/O backed streams, closing is mandatory.

cards.front: Which method streams the split result of a regex without building an intermediate array?
cards.back: Pattern.compile(re).splitAsStream(text)
cards.extra: String.split first builds an array of all pieces, which wastes memory and CPU when the pipeline is short-circuited before consuming everything.

cards.front: What happens if you add elements to a Stream.builder() after building a stream from it?
cards.back: IllegalStateException
cards.extra: A builder is single-use: once it has produced a stream, it cannot be reused or extended. Build the complete element set first.

cards.front: Which factory produces the body handler that streams an HTTP response line by line?
cards.back: HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofLines()
cards.extra: The handler, part of the HTTP Client API added in JDK 11, gives a Stream<String> without holding the body in memory.

cards.front: Name the four components a collector can be built from.
cards.back: supplier, accumulator, combiner, and finisher
cards.extra: The first two collect elements; the combiner merges partial containers in parallel; the finisher post-processes the container into the result type.

cards.front: What interfaces model the supplier and accumulator of a collector?
cards.back: Supplier creates the container; BiConsumer adds one element to it
cards.extra: The accumulator takes the partially filled container and the element. Its name in the Collector API is the accumulator, mirroring the reduce stage of the collector pipeline.

cards.front: When is a combiner needed?
cards.back: For parallel streams, to merge one container per substream into one
cards.extra: Each thread fills its own container from the same supplier, then the combiner (a BinaryOperator) merges the two. A sequential stream never calls it.

cards.front: What does the finisher do that the supplier and accumulator cannot?
cards.back: Turns the mutable container into the final result type
cards.extra: Its classic use is sealing an intermediate container into an immutable list, set or map, or converting a StringBuffer into a String.

cards.front: For Stream.collect(supplier, acc, combiner) versus a Collector, how do the combiner types differ?
cards.back: The three-argument collect takes a BiConsumer; Collector.of takes a BinaryOperator
cards.extra: The BiConsumer form merges two containers and returns nothing; the BinaryOperator form returns the merged container for further use.

cards.front: For which streams does collect(supplier, acc, combiner) exist in a primitive form?
cards.back: The numeric streams, e.g. IntStream.collect
cards.extra: There the accumulator is an ObjIntConsumer so the int arrives without boxing. The Collectors factory class, by contrast, only serves object streams.

cards.front: Why can't a collector accumulate into a String directly?
cards.back: String is immutable, so there is nothing to append to
cards.extra: Use StringBuffer or StringBuilder as the mutable container and convert in the finisher. That is exactly how Collectors.joining works internally.

cards.front: What does the collectingAndThen() finisher enable?
cards.back: Applying a post-processing function to the result of another collector
cards.extra: Its main use is converting a finished collector into something reusable: the whole operation becomes one collector, so it can serve as a downstream of another.

cards.front: What does the teeing() collector do, and when did it arrive?
cards.back: Collects in two downstream collectors at once and merges with a bifunction; Java SE 12
cards.extra: Data is processed in a single pass, so two independent results cost one traversal. Typical use: collect some items and count them together.

cards.front: How many arguments does teeing() take?
cards.back: Three: two downstream collectors and a merging bifunction
cards.extra: Each downstream builds its own container from the same stream, and the bifunction combines those two containers into the final result.

cards.front: Since which JDK version is the Gatherer API available, and what does it model?
cards.back: JDK 24 - it models intermediate operations on a stream
cards.extra: Design-wise it mirrors the Collector API, which is for terminal operations. A gatherer is passed to the Stream method gather().

cards.front: Which two main elements is the Gatherer API built on?
cards.back: The Gatherer interface and the Gatherers factory class
cards.extra: The interface is functional, so a gatherer can be a lambda; the factory class supplies ready-made gatherers such as fold, scan and the windowing ones.

cards.front: Should you replace map() with a hand-written gatherer for performance?
cards.back: No - the built-in methods are simpler and far more readable
cards.extra: The Gatherer API exists for operations the Stream API does not offer. Fusing stages into a gatherer creates fewer objects, but needs measurement and hurts readability.

cards.front: What are the upstream and downstream of a gatherer?
cards.back: Upstream: the stream elements come from; downstream: the stream it pushes to
cards.extra: An integrator consumes from upstream and pushes to downstream; the types on the two sides may differ, since a gatherer may map.

cards.front: What three elements does the abstract method of Integrator take?
cards.back: The internal state, the upstream element, and the downstream
cards.extra: Its type <A, T, R> is state, consumed and produced type. Its boolean result signals whether the upstream should stop producing.

cards.front: What does the boolean returned by downstream.push() mean?
cards.back: false means the downstream no longer accepts elements
cards.extra: Returning that value from the integrator lets the API stop calling it. It must be passed through unchanged, since a downstream can never reopen.

cards.front: State the three rules about a downstream's rejecting state.
cards.back: Starts accepting; can only switch to rejecting; only when you push
cards.extra: So a fresh downstream never starts rejecting, even if the call is followed by limit(0). A rejecting downstream stays rejecting forever.

cards.front: Where do you need to check isRejecting(): in the integrator or the finisher?
cards.back: In the finisher only
cards.extra: In an integrator the downstream cannot be rejecting when the call begins, since the previous push told you the state. The finisher runs later and may need the test.

cards.front: What happens if you push elements to a rejecting downstream?
cards.back: They are silently ignored - no exception, only wasted work
cards.extra: Sensible gatherers return the push result upstream so the source stops early; ignoring it costs whatever the extra computation involves.

cards.front: Which factory method creates a gatherer with an initializer for mutable state?
cards.back: Gatherer.ofSequential(initializer, integrator)
cards.extra: Use ofSequential when the gatherer cannot run in parallel; Gatherer.of with four arguments is the parallel-capable form that also needs a combiner.

cards.front: Why is a @SafeVarargs-style care needed when flattening with flatMapper.apply(x).forEach(downstream::push)?
cards.back: The returned stream may be parallel, and Downstream is not thread-safe
cards.extra: Calling sequential() on the returned stream removes the race. A stream must also be closed, so try-with-resources belongs here.

cards.front: What does a greedy integrator commit to?
cards.back: It never interrupts on its own: it returns the downstream state or true
cards.extra: Declared with Integrator.ofGreedy, it lets the API apply optimizations. Breaking the contract can make the code fail; a greedy plain integrator only misses optimizations.

cards.front: Why does a gatherer that must see all elements before emitting, such as a sort, need a finisher?
cards.back: Nothing else tells it the upstream is exhausted
cards.extra: The finisher runs once when no more elements arrive. For sorting, the integrator stores elements in a buffer and the finisher pushes them in order.

cards.front: Which type models a gatherer's finisher?
cards.back: BiConsumer<State, Downstream>
cards.extra: It takes the state and the downstream and returns nothing. A gatherer with no state uses Void as the state type and ignores that argument.

cards.front: Which Gatherer.of signature declares mutable state and a combiner for parallel use?
cards.back: of(initializer, integrator, combiner, finisher)
cards.extra: The combiner (a BinaryOperator) merges two state instances. Mutable state is never shared between threads, so no locks are needed.

cards.front: How much parallelism does a sequential gatherer leave in a parallel stream?
cards.back: Stages before gather() still run in parallel; the gatherer runs single-threaded
cards.extra: Only the gatherer stage is serialized, which is a benefit unique to the Gatherer API - a Spliterator-based custom stage would kill parallelism entirely.

cards.front: Which method composes two gatherers into one?
cards.back: andThen() on the Gatherer interface
cards.extra: The first gatherer's produced type must match the second's consumed type. It replaces writing one monolithic integrator for two stages.

cards.front: What is the difference between the fold() and scan() factory gatherers?
