cards.back: fold pushes only the final result; scan pushes every intermediate value
cards.extra: Both apply a BiFunction element by element. fold acts like reduce inside an intermediate operation; scan emits the running accumulation at each step.

cards.front: What does the mapConcurrent() gatherer use to run each mapping, and what limits it?
cards.back: Virtual threads, capped by the maxConcurrency argument
cards.extra: It consumes all elements then maps each on its own virtual thread. Despite the concurrency it is a sequential gatherer, made with Gatherer.ofSequential.

cards.front: How do the fixed and sliding window gatherers differ?
cards.back: Fixed windows are disjoint; sliding windows advance by one
cards.extra: Fixed: [0,1,2][3,4,5], and the last may be short. Sliding: [0,1,2][1,2,3], all of equal size, each element in several windows.

cards.front: On what kind of stream is a windowing gatherer meaningless?
cards.back: A non-ORDERED stream
cards.extra: A window is an interval of indexes, so without order two runs over the same data may produce different windows or inconsistent results.

cards.front: What does a pipeline with only map() and no terminal operation do?
cards.back: Nothing - no data is processed
cards.extra: Intermediate operations only build the pipeline. A missing terminal operation is a bug, and no element will ever flow.

cards.front: What do mapToInt, mapToLong, mapToDouble produce?
cards.back: Specialized primitive streams: IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream
cards.extra: They avoid boxing and unlock primitive-only terminal operations such as sum() and summaryStatistics(), which plain Stream does not have.

cards.front: Which terminal operation gives count, min, max, sum and average in one pass?
cards.back: summaryStatistics() on a primitive stream
cards.extra: It returns an IntSummaryStatistics-like object rather than a value. It only exists on the numeric streams, not on Stream<Integer>.

cards.front: What does flatMap() do in two steps?
cards.back: Maps each element to a stream, then flattens all those streams into one
cards.extra: It turns Stream<Country> into Stream<Stream<City>> and then into Stream<City>. This is the one-to-many operation of the API.

cards.front: Why is flatMap better than a stream inside a for loop?
cards.back: It expresses the one-to-many relation in the pipeline, with no nested iteration
cards.extra: A stream created inside a loop does not fit the map-filter-reduce model and cannot be optimized with the rest of the pipeline.

cards.front: How does a flat-mapper drop invalid elements, e.g. unparsable integers?
cards.back: Return an empty stream for invalid elements, a single-element stream otherwise
cards.extra: This try/catch-in-the-mapper pattern is safer than a predicate filter, which must parse twice and cannot catch the exception cleanly.

cards.front: Which method replaced the empty-stream flat-map idiom in Java SE 16?
cards.back: mapMulti(BiConsumer)
cards.extra: The biconsumer receives the element and a consumer; it calls that consumer only for values it wants to emit, so no extra stream is created per element.

cards.front: What type must you state for mapMulti, and what happens if you omit it?
cards.back: The result type of the emitting consumer; omitted, it is assumed Stream<Object>
cards.extra: The compiler cannot infer from a BiConsumer alone, so give an explicit type on its parameter or write <Integer>mapMulti(...).

cards.front: Why are distinct() and sorted() exceptions to 'a stream stores no data'?
cards.back: They must buffer elements: a set of seen values, and a sortable buffer
cards.extra: distinct still streams: it pushes an element immediately the first time it is seen. sorted must collect everything before emitting anything.

cards.front: Can distinct() or sorted() be used on an unbounded stream?
cards.back: distinct can, sorted cannot
cards.extra: distinct emits as it discovers new values, so a limit downstream can end the infinite source. sorted can never emit without seeing the end.

cards.front: Which two methods select elements by index, and which two by predicate?
cards.back: Index: skip(n), limit(n). Predicate: dropWhile(p), takeWhile(p)
cards.extra: The predicate pair arrived in Java SE 9. takeWhile is the functional break; dropWhile is its mirror image.

cards.front: On Stream.of(1,2,3,4,5,6,7), what does skip(2).limit(5) yield?
cards.back: 3 4 5 6 7 - limit counts on the new stream
cards.extra: skip produces a stream starting at 3, so its first 5 elements end at 7. Each intermediate call sees only the stream handed to it.

cards.front: Which factory method concatenates two streams, and what is the recommended alternative for more?
cards.back: Stream.concat(a, b); for three or more, flatMap over a stream of streams
cards.extra: concat produces a SIZED stream but creates throwaway intermediate streams per call, so chaining several of them wastes objects.

cards.front: What does Stream.concat preserve that a flatMap concatenation loses?
cards.back: concat keeps the stream SIZED; flatMap does not
cards.extra: With known source sizes, the concatenated size is simply their sum. flatMap may emit an unknown number of elements per input.

cards.front: What is peek() for, and why avoid it in production?
cards.back: Debugging a pipeline stage; it must not be used for side effects
cards.extra: It shows each element passing through. Side-effect logic in peek may be skipped by the optimizer when the stream short-circuits, so it is unreliable.

cards.front: Does stream processing follow element-at-a-time traversal?
cards.back: Yes - each element passes through all stages before the next enters
cards.extra: peek makes this visible: element 1 is filtered out, element 2 is mapped and added, and no stage handles a whole list at once.

cards.front: Which three steps does the map-filter-reduce algorithm consist of?
cards.back: Select elements, transform them, then aggregate to one result
cards.extra: The classic example: keep October sales, map each to its amount, sum the amounts. Every stream pipeline is a variant of these three.

cards.front: What does mapping change about the objects, and what does filtering change?
cards.back: Mapping changes types one-to-one; filtering changes the number, keeping types
cards.extra: Map ten objects and you get ten results. Filter ten and you may get fewer. Map is a Function, filter a Predicate.

cards.front: Which functional interfaces model the mapping and filtering steps?
cards.back: Function for map, Predicate for filter
cards.extra: Both return a stream in the pipeline. Specialized variants such as ToIntFunction exist to avoid boxing primitives.

cards.front: Why are map() and filter() on Stream and not on Collection?
cards.back: Returning a collection would force eager intermediate structures
cards.extra: Each stage would build and store a whole collection. A stream is an empty object that carries no data, so the stages are free until a terminal operation pulls.

cards.front: Complete the key property: a stream is an object that ...
cards.back: ... does not store any data
cards.extra: Data is pulled from the source element by element only when a terminal operation runs, so no intermediate list exists in a pure pipeline.

cards.front: What is the difference between an intermediate and a terminal operation?
cards.back: Intermediate returns a stream; terminal returns anything else, including void
cards.extra: Only a terminal operation triggers consumption. Invoking any operation makes the stream consumed for good.

cards.front: What happens if you call a second operation on an already-used stream?
cards.back: IllegalStateException: "stream has already been operated upon or closed"
cards.extra: A stream is single use, so s.map(f).toList() then s.count() fails. Create streams on the spot instead of storing them in fields.

cards.front: Which terminal operations exist only on IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream?
cards.back: sum(), min(), max(), average(), summaryStatistics()
cards.extra: They avoid boxing by working on primitives throughout. On Stream<Integer> you would use reduce() with a binary operator instead.

cards.front: Why should a stream source not be modified while the stream runs?
cards.back: The result becomes unspecified
cards.extra: Streams pull from a live source, so a concurrent modification can skip, duplicate or fail to see elements. Copy the data if you must change it.

cards.front: Which two coding practices does the single-use rule make dangerous?
cards.back: Storing streams in fields or locals, and passing them as method arguments
cards.extra: The callee cannot know whether the stream was already consumed, so it may throw. A stream should be created and consumed in one place.

cards.front: What is an Optional<T>?
cards.back: A wrapper that either holds a value or is empty
cards.extra: Its point of difference from Integer or Long is emptiness. It signals to the method's caller that no result may exist, replacing null returns.

cards.front: Which three factory methods create an Optional?
cards.back: empty(), of(x), ofNullable(x)
cards.extra: Optional has no public constructor and is final, so these are the only ways. of() throws on null; ofNullable() gives an empty optional instead.

cards.front: What happens if you pass null to Optional.of()?
cards.back: NullPointerException - use ofNullable for possibly null input
cards.extra: That restriction guarantees the invariant: an optional that is not empty always wraps a non-null reference. Opening it can never give null back.

cards.front: Which primitive optionals exist, and why is there no ofNullable on them?
cards.back: OptionalInt, OptionalLong, OptionalDouble; a primitive cannot be null
cards.extra: They wrap values, not references, so only empty(), of(value) and simple accessors apply. They pair with the specialized numeric streams.

cards.front: Which two methods test an optional, and since when does isEmpty() exist?
cards.back: isPresent() and isEmpty(), the latter since Java SE 11
cards.extra: They serve the same purpose; isEmpty reads better in guard clauses. Neither gives access to the content.

cards.front: How do orElse and orElseGet differ?
cards.back: orElse(v) always evaluates v; orElseGet(supplier) calls it only when needed
cards.extra: For cheap literals orElse is fine. For an expensive object, orElseGet avoids building one that would be discarded, which can matter in hot code.

cards.front: Why is orElseThrow() preferred over get()?
cards.back: Its name warns that an empty optional throws NoSuchElementException
cards.extra: Java SE 10 added it because get() looked like a harmless getter. get() remains for compatibility but is deprecated.

cards.front: What does optional.or(supplier) return?
cards.back: This optional if it is not empty; otherwise the optional built by the supplier
cards.extra: Unlike orElse, the fallback is itself an Optional, so emptiness is preserved rather than replaced by a default value.

cards.front: How does Optional.flatMap differ from Optional.map?
cards.back: map's function returns a value; flatMap's returns an Optional
cards.extra: map wraps the result in an Optional, and flatMap avoids Optional<Optional<T>>. Both short-circuit to empty when the source is empty.

cards.front: What does optional.stream() give you, and why is it useful?
cards.back: A stream of zero or one element, letting optionals enter a stream pipeline
cards.extra: Inside flatMap the empty streams simply vanish, which is the standard idiom for filtering out empty optionals in one pass.

cards.front: What is the difference between ifPresent and ifPresentOrElse?
cards.back: ifPresentOrElse also takes a Runnable to run when empty
cards.extra: ifPresent maps to Stream.forEach, so it handles only the value case. The two-argument form gives an explicit else branch.

cards.front: Which rule forbids orElseThrow() without a check?
cards.back: Rule #2: never open an optional unless you are sure it is not empty
cards.extra: Rule #3 adds that you should prefer alternatives to ifPresent, orElseThrow or get. Both exist because opening is the risky operation.

cards.front: What do Optionals rules #5 and #7 say?
cards.back: #5: not in fields, parameters, collections or maps. #7: not serializable
cards.extra: Optional is a return-type tool. Using it as a field or argument adds a wrapper everywhere and still cannot be serialized, so it breaks persistence.

cards.front: What does Optional rule #4 say about null checks?
cards.back: Do not create an optional just to avoid testing a reference for null
cards.extra: If a variable may be null and the type is a field or parameter, the correct fix is to redesign the API, not to wrap it in Optional at every touch point.

cards.front: Which single method makes a stream compute in parallel?
cards.back: parallel(), on any existing stream
cards.extra: It needs no pool setup and no thread code. Whether it improves anything depends on the data and the workload, so it must be measured.

cards.front: Is a parallel stream always faster than a sequential one?
cards.back: No - parallelizing adds splitting, merging and thread overhead
cards.extra: It wins only when the work per element is heavy, the source splits cheaply and evenly, and free cores exist. Measure against production-like data.

cards.front: On what framework is parallel stream computation built?
cards.back: The Fork/Join framework using the common pool (JDK 7 onward)
cards.extra: The sourcу is recursively decomposed in halves, each part processed on a core, and the partial results merged with the same operator.

cards.front: Why is an ArrayList good for parallel streams and a LinkedList bad?
cards.back: Array slices split in constant time; finding a linked list's middle is linear
cards.extra: A LinkedList also causes pointer chasing. ArrayList, TreeSet and IntStream.range split evenly; LinkedList and HashSet do not.

cards.front: What is pointer chasing, and where does it hurt most?
cards.back: Following references to reach data; worst for LinkedList<Integer>
cards.extra: An array of ints needs no chasing, an array of Integer needs one hop per element, and a linked list needs two per node, so cache misses multiply.

cards.front: Why is a 64-byte cache line relevant to stream performance?
cards.back: Memory is copied line by line, so neighbouring values come for free
cards.extra: A 64-byte line holds 16 ints or 8 longs, so iterating a primitive array pays one cache miss per line instead of one per value.

cards.front: What is work stealing in the Fork/Join framework?
cards.back: An idle thread takes tasks from another thread's queue
cards.extra: Splitting one task leaves the others idle, so they grab subtasks. It keeps all cores busy but makes the processing order unpredictable.

cards.front: Which methods are stateful and need the encounter order in a parallel stream?
cards.back: limit(n), skip(n) and findFirst()
cards.extra: They count or track position, so a shared internal counter is required across threads, which is costly and hard to parallelize effectively.

cards.front: Which anti-pattern is the classic source of wrong results in a parallel stream?
cards.back: Adding to a shared, non-thread-safe collection from the pipeline
cards.extra: All threads write into one ArrayList concurrently, so elements are lost and an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is possible. Use a collector instead.

cards.front: What are the four overheads of computing a stream in parallel?
cards.back: Splitting, work dispatch, per-part processing, and merging partial results
cards.extra: Merging a sum is cheap; merging hash maps is not. If the total exceeds the gain from parallelism, the parallel stream is slower.

cards.front: Why does the Fork/Join common pool raise concerns in a web server?
cards.back: Its threads are shared, so blocking work can starve other parallel tasks
cards.extra: The pool is sized to the number of cores and shared JVM-wide. Long blocking operations should not run there.

cards.front: What does the first rule of parallelizing say?
cards.back: Optimize because you have requirements you do not meet, not for fun
cards.extra: Rule #3 adds: do not modify external state or share mutable state. Rule #4: measure, never guess.

cards.front: How many overloads does Stream.reduce() have, and what do they all take?
cards.back: Three; each takes a binary operator (directly or through a mapper)
cards.extra: The variants differ in whether they take an identity element, and whether they also fuse a mapping step.

cards.front: What does a reduction do to a stream of elements?
cards.back: Combines them pairwise with a binary operator until one value remains
cards.extra: Sum: take the first two, add; take the next, add to the partial; repeat. Any operator of that shape can reduce, yielding sum, max or concatenation.

cards.front: What property must a binary operator passed to reduce() have, and why?
cards.back: Associativity - so splitting the data cannot change the result
cards.extra: (3+6)+(2+1) and 3+(6+2+1) must agree, since parallel processing splits the source arbitrarily. The API is silent about violations.

cards.front: What happens if a non-associative operator is passed to reduce()?
cards.back: Nothing detectable - results may silently differ run to run
cards.extra: Neither compiler nor runtime checks it. Testing with random data can prove the operator wrong, but cannot prove it right.

cards.front: What is the identity element of a reduction, in words?
cards.back: The value that leaves every other value unchanged when combined
cards.extra: For + it is 0, for * it is 1, for max it is minus infinity. The reduction of an empty set is the identity element.

cards.front: Why do MIN and MAX need special handling in a reduction?
cards.back: They have no identity element, so an empty stream has no result
cards.extra: The API wraps such results in an Optional, which is empty if the stream was empty and leaves the choice to you.

cards.front: What does the reduce(identity, op) overload return, and what does reduce(op) return?
cards.back: With identity: a plain value; without: an Optional
cards.extra: The identity lets the API skip reading the first element and start from it, so an empty stream returns the identity instead of nothing.

cards.front: What happens if the value you pass as the identity is wrong?
cards.back: A silently corrupted result - no error, no exception
cards.extra: The implementation starts the algorithm from your value, so a wrong one shifts every intermediate result. The API trusts your claim completely.

cards.front: What does the three-argument reduce overload fuse together?
cards.back: A mapping and a reduction into one accumulator step
cards.extra: Signature: reduce(U identity, BiFunction<U, ? super T, U> accumulator, BinaryOperator combiner). U is the accumulating type.

cards.front: In the three-argument reduce, which element must be the identity's match?
cards.back: The combiner's identity, not the accumulator's
cards.extra: The combiner merges partial results of type U, so its identity sets what the reduction returns for an empty stream.

cards.front: Which overload should you use when reducing with a non-associative but reasonable operator?
cards.back: None - use a sequential collect or a gatherer such as fold instead
cards.extra: Gatherer.fold() was added precisely for cases without a combiner. reduce keeps its contract: associative operator only.
